segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days John the Baptist came, proclaiming in the wilderness of Judea

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is the one spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, who said:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “A voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now John himself wore clothing made of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan were going out to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they were being baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So produce fruit worthy of turning back,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Already the ax is laid at the root of the trees; so every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I baptize you in water for turning back, but the one coming after me is stronger than I am, and I am not fit to carry his sandals. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: His winnowing shovel is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But John tried to stop him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Allow it for now, for in this way it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he allowed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had been baptized, he came up at once from the water; and look, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, a voice from the heavens, saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “This is my Son, the beloved, with whom I am well pleased.”

notes.note: The traditional rendering is “repent,” which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word, as used in the Gospels, carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. The related noun in verses 8 and 11 is rendered “turning back.”

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that most translations flatten to “heaven.” The expression is characteristic of Matthew and is generally understood as equivalent to “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels, with “the heavens” standing reverently for God.

The Greek perfect tense says that the kingdom has drawn near and now stands close. Whether this means it is about to arrive or has in some sense already arrived is debated; the rendering leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

notes.phrase: A voice of one crying out in the wilderness
notes.note: The quotation is Isaiah 40:3 in the form found in the Greek translation of the Scriptures (the Septuagint). In the Hebrew text “in the wilderness” more naturally goes with “prepare the way”; the Greek form, attaching it to the voice, fits John’s location. “His paths” replaces Isaiah’s “the paths of our God.”

notes.phrase: a leather belt around his waist
notes.note: John’s dress recalls the description of the prophet Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8, a hairy garment and a leather belt. A reader who knew the Scriptures would have caught the allusion, which Matthew later makes explicit when Jesus identifies John with Elijah.

The Greek can mean that they came in order to be baptized or simply that they came to the place where John was baptizing, perhaps to observe. John’s sharp response fits either reading, and the rendering keeps the Greek’s openness.

The Greek preposition can mark either the element in which someone is immersed (“in”) or the means used (“with”), and translations are divided. “In” is chosen because the verb’s ordinary sense is to dip or immerse; the same preposition is rendered the same way for “in the Holy Spirit and fire.”
Carrying or removing a master’s sandals was a task for a slave. John is saying he is not worthy to perform even the lowliest service for the one who is coming.

Most modern translations have “winnowing fork,” but the Greek word names the shovel used to toss threshed grain into the wind so that the light chaff blows away and the heavier grain falls to the floor; a different word was used for the fork. The image is the same either way: the harvest is in and the separation is about to begin.

Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). In Matthew the word usually refers to doing what God requires, and here most interpreters take “fulfill all righteousness” to mean carrying out everything God’s will calls for. Some see instead a reference to God’s saving plan being brought to completion.

notes.traditional: the heavens were opened to him
notes.note: Many manuscripts add “to him” after “opened,” while some important early witnesses lack it. The text translated here follows the shorter reading; the difference affects whether the opening is presented as something Jesus in particular perceived.

The words echo Psalm 2:7 (“You are my son”) and Isaiah 42:1 (the servant in whom God delights). In the Greek Scriptures “beloved” used of a son can carry the nuance of an only child, as with Isaac in Genesis 22:2.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the New Testament and translators divide between “preach” and “proclaim,” with “preach” now suggesting a sermon rather than a herald’s announcement.
Translations vary between “wilderness,” “desert,” and “deserted place,” and the choice affects the echo of Israel’s wilderness traditions across the Gospels.
The perfect ἤγγικεν in kingdom sayings is rendered “is at hand,” “has come near,” or “is near” and needs one form across the Synoptics.
Extremely frequent attention-marker rendered variously as “behold,” “look,” “see,” “suddenly,” or omitted; a uniform policy is needed.
The heavenly-voice sayings at the baptism and transfiguration recur across the Gospels and 2 Peter and should match; options include “am well pleased,” “delight,” and “take pleasure.”
